title: AI Finds Hidden Osteoporosis in Everyday CT Scans, Study Shows
source_used: Scienmag (text read on the Bioengineer.org copy)
key_facts: A team at Changzheng Hospital of Naval Medical University in Shanghai published the study in BMC Medical Imaging.
It was a retrospective study of 518 patients who had both DXA (the standard bone-density scan) and a lumbar non-contrast CT.
Commercial AI software segmented the vertebrae and measured volumetric bone mineral density from T12 to L2; four ways of combining the vertebrae were compared.
The four AI methods agreed closely with each other (ICC 0.909), and agreed with DXA less closely (ICCs 0.649 to 0.689).
For flagging osteoporosis the AI had precision 0.834 and recall 0.735, so about 83 percent of its flags were right and it caught roughly three-quarters of true cases.
Averaging density over T12, L1 and L2 performed best.
The study was single-centre and retrospective, used one commercial product, and needs validation across populations and scanner types.
quote_evidence: Their retrospective study enrolled 518 patients who had undergone both DXA and lumbar non-contrast CT, allowing direct comparison of the two modalities in the same individuals.

Here the AI achieved a precision of 0.834—meaning that when it flags a patient as osteoporotic, it is right about 83 percent of the time—and a recall of 0.735, meaning it catches roughly three-quarters of true osteoporosis cases.
Cautions remain, as they must with any retrospective, single-center study.
why_it_matters_hint: Scans taken for other reasons could double as a bone-density check at no extra radiation or visit, but about one in four cases was missed in this single-centre study.
event_date: Scienmag article dated 10 Oct 2026; study publication date not stated
